key_history.title: Roanoke Island and the English colonial expeditions
key_history.summary: Roanoke Island was the site of English voyages and settlement attempts in the 1580s. The 1587 group led by John White remained on the island after its planned journey to the Chesapeake did not proceed. White returned in 1590 and found the settlement no longer present; the colonists' fate remains unresolved.
key_history.source_name: National Park Service — Fort Raleigh National Historic Site

key_history.title: Roanoke Island Freedmen's Colony
key_history.summary: After Union forces took Roanoke Island in February 1862, freedom seekers arrived and a community developed. The colony included homes, churches, schools, and other institutions. The federal government restored confiscated land after the war, and the colony was officially decommissioned by 1867. Its history is part of the island's story beyond the earlier English expeditions.
key_history.source_name: National Park Service — The Freedmen's Colony on Roanoke Island

halifax-county.seo_description: Explore the Halifax Resolves of April 12, 1776, and their role in North Carolina's path to independence, with a source from the North Carolina General Assembly.

key_history.title: The Halifax Resolves
key_history.summary: The Fourth Provincial Congress meeting at Halifax adopted the Halifax Resolves, instructing North Carolina's delegates to the Continental Congress to concur with the other colonies in declaring independence from Great Britain. It was the first official action by a colony authorizing its delegates to vote for independence.
key_history.source_name: North Carolina General Assembly — Halifax Resolves

key_history.summary: Salem was founded in 1766 as the central town of the Moravian Wachovia settlement. Old Salem Museums & Gardens preserves and interprets the community's history through historic sites, collections, and research resources.

key_history.title: Tryon Palace and colonial government
key_history.summary: Tryon Palace opened in New Bern in 1770 and served as the residence of royal governors and a center of colonial government. It became colonial North Carolina's first permanent capitol building; the site is now interpreted by Tryon Palace as a historic place.
